title: He Wasted His Father’s Money on Wild Living — Then He Came Home Expecting Rejection
paragraphs: He Wasted His Father’s Money on Wild Living — Then He Came Home Expecting Rejection

He had already rehearsed the speech that would reduce him from son to servant. But before he could finish it, his father was running toward him. And if you have ever wondered whether you have sinned too badly, wandered too far, wasted too much, or disappointed God too deeply to come home, Jesus told this story for people exactly like you.
He could probably see the house before anyone in the house could see him.
And that may have been the hardest part.
Every step toward home carried another memory.
The road he once walked with money in his pocket, dreams in his head, and freedom burning in his chest was now the road of his humiliation.
He had left as somebody.
He was returning with nothing.
No inheritance.
No impressive story.
No evidence that his rebellion had somehow worked out.
Nothing to show his father except the wreckage of everything his father had entrusted to him.
Maybe you know that road.
Maybe your "far country" never appeared on a map.
Maybe you never disappeared geographically. You still went to work. Still answered messages. Still smiled in photographs. Still said, "I'm fine."
But somewhere inside, you left home.
Maybe your far country was pornography nobody knew about.
Maybe it was an affair.
Maybe it was alcohol.
Maybe it was bitterness you kept feeding while pretending you had forgiven.
Maybe it was money.
Attention.
Pride.
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you didn't run from God dramatically.
You simply stopped listening.
Stopped praying.
Stopped opening Scripture.
Stopped feeling bothered by what once convicted you.
And eventually you learned one of sin's oldest lessons:
The far country always advertises freedom before revealing the bill.
Jesus tells this story in Luke 15, and the setting matters.

Tax collectors and people publicly regarded as sinners were gathering around Jesus, while Pharisees and scribes complained that He welcomed sinners and ate with them. Jesus answered their grumbling with three stories about what was lost and what was found: a sheep, a coin, and finally a son.
Then Jesus begins:
Ἄνθρωπός τις εἶχεν δύο υἱούς.
Anthrōpos tis eichen dyo huious.
Literally: "A certain man had two sons."
Two sons.
Remember that.
Because this is not merely a story about one reckless young man.
Jesus is going after the hearts of sinners and religious people.
One son becomes lost far away.
The other will eventually reveal that a person can be lost while standing frighteningly close to the father's house.
But first comes the scandal everyone remembers.
The younger son asks for his share of the property.
He wants what belongs to him without remaining under his father's roof.
He wants the father's possessions more than the father's presence.
And that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because isn't that one of the deepest forms of human rebellion?
"God, give me life—but don't govern it."
"Give me love—but don't tell me whom to love."
"Give me a body—but don't tell me what holiness looks like."
"Give me money—but don't tell me what to do with it."
"Give me success—but don't ask for the glory."
"Give me another morning—but don't ask me to surrender the day."
We want the Father's gifts while resisting the Father's authority.
The younger son receives his portion, gathers everything together, travels into a distant country, and wastes what he has.
Luke describes his manner of living with a devastating Greek word:
ἀσώτως — asōtōs.
It carries the sense of reckless, wasteful, dissolute living.
This was not merely a young man who made a poor investment.
He was unraveling.
He took what had been given in love and burned through it in rebellion.
And sin still works like that.
Sin rarely announces itself by saying, "I have come to destroy you."
It says:
"You deserve this."
"Just once."
"Nobody will know."
"You can stop whenever you want."
"God understands."
"You've been good long enough."
"This will finally make you happy."
Then one day you discover that what promised to serve you has become your master.
The money disappeared.
Then the circumstances changed.
A severe famine came.
And suddenly the people, pleasures, and possibilities surrounding the young man could not save him.
Jesus brings him lower and lower until this Jewish son is feeding pigs and longing for their food.
Think about the humiliation.
The boy who demanded his inheritance is now hungry beside swine.
The hands that once held his father's wealth are now surrounded by pig food.
The freedom he demanded has become bondage.
And there, somewhere beneath the shame, something happens.
Luke 15:17 contains one of the most beautiful descriptions of awakening in Scripture:
εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν
eis heauton de elthōn
In a very literal sense:
"But having come to himself..."
He came to himself.
Sin had taken him so far from the man he was created to be that repentance began to feel like waking up.
This is one reason biblical repentance is so much more beautiful than mere religious shame.
Shame says, "Hide."
Pride says, "Excuse it."
Culture may say, "Redefine it."
Despair says, "It's too late."
Repentance says, "I will arise and go to my father."
The son finally tells the truth.
No excuses.
No blaming his friends.
No blaming the famine.
No blaming his upbringing.
No carefully edited explanation designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
He knows he has sinned.
So he prepares his confession.
He will tell his father that he has sinned against heaven and before him and is no longer worthy to be called his son.
Then he develops a survival plan.
Make me like one of your hired servants.
That part matters.
Because he is returning home, but he still doesn't understand the father's heart.
He believes the best possible ending is employment.
He expects consequences without intimacy.
Survival without sonship.
Bread without belonging.
Perhaps that is where some people reading this are living right now.
You believe Jesus can forgive other people.
You believe grace theoretically.
You sing about mercy.
You share Bible verses.
But when your own secret failure comes to mind, something inside whispers:
"Not you."
"You knew better."
"You've done this too many times."
"After everything God gave you?"
"After all your promises?"
"Maybe God will tolerate you, but He could never delight in you again."
So you start negotiating like the younger son.
"I'll work harder."
"I'll prove myself."
"I'll punish myself."
"I'll become religious enough to compensate for what I did."
But then Jesus changes the entire emotional direction of the story.
The son is still far away when his father sees him.
That detail should stop you.
While he was still far away.
The father sees him.
Then Luke uses an extraordinary word:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplagchnisthē.
He was moved with deep compassion.
This is not the picture of a cold father reluctantly agreeing to process a sinner's application for reinstatement. The language communicates profound, visceral compassion.
And then—
the father runs.
The son had rehearsed a speech.
The father had compassion.
The son expected distance.
The father closed it.
The son expected anger.
The father embraced him.
The son expected to negotiate.
The father kissed him.
Can you see him?
Dirty.
Hungry.
Ashamed.
Probably smelling like the life he had just escaped.
And his father does not stand on the porch shouting:
"Clean yourself up first!"
He runs toward him.
This does not mean the son's rebellion did not matter.
It mattered enough to bring him to ruin.
Grace never requires us to pretend sin is harmless.
The son confesses that he has sinned.
Jesus Himself frames Luke 15 around repentance; earlier in the chapter He speaks of heaven rejoicing over one sinner who repents.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is God receiving the repentant sinner who has finally stopped calling evil good.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not:
"Live however you want because God forgives."
The Gospel is infinitely more glorious:

You have sinned against a holy God. You cannot save yourself. Yet God has acted in mercy through Jesus Christ. Christ bore sin, died, and rose again; forgiveness is offered to sinners who turn to Him in repentant faith.
The Father's house is not reached by pretending the far country was beautiful.
You come home by admitting it was killing you.
And look at what happens next.
The son begins his confession.
But before he can turn his return into a plan for earning his place, the father starts giving orders.
Bring the best robe.
Put a ring on his hand.
Put shoes on his feet.
Prepare the feast.
Why?
Because, in the father's words, his son was dead and is alive again.
He was lost and has been found.
Notice the language.
Not:
"My employee has returned."
Not:
"The disappointment is back."
Not:
"Let's keep him outside for six months and see whether he deserves another chance."
My son.
The boy came home carrying a servant's speech.
The father answered with signs of restoration.
That is grace.
And grace is scandalous precisely because it cannot be purchased by the person who desperately needs it.
The prodigal had no money left to buy his restoration.
He had already wasted his resources.
All he could bring home was repentance.
The father supplied the celebration.
And here the story points beyond itself toward the heart of the Gospel.
We do not reconcile ourselves to God by accumulating enough religious merit to cancel our sins.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, grace does not ignore justice.
Christ bears judgment.
At the empty tomb, death does not get the final word.
Christ rises.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at your sin.
It is God providing in His Son what sinners could never provide for themselves.
You do not clean yourself up enough to make Christ willing to receive you.
You come because you need Christ to save you.
Maybe you have wasted years.
Come home.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Come home—and be willing to walk through the costly work of repentance and rebuilding.
Maybe you have been hiding an addiction.
Bring it into the light and come home.
Maybe your marriage bears scars from your selfishness.
Repent and come home.
Maybe you have money but no peace.
Come home.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are strong, while privately you feel spiritually numb.
Come home.
Maybe you returned to the same sin after swearing before God that you never would.
Do not turn repeated failure into permission to keep sinning.
Repent.
Seek help.
Cut off what feeds the sin.
Confess where confession is biblically appropriate.
And run to Christ.
Come home.
But Jesus isn't finished.
There is another son.
The older brother hears the celebration and becomes angry.
He has remained near the house.
He has worked.
He has obeyed outwardly.
Yet when grace is poured over his broken brother, his heart exposes itself.
He cannot celebrate mercy because he thinks relationship with his father operates like wages.
He essentially argues from his record.
Look how long I served.
Look what I did.
Look what I never did.
And suddenly we realize:
There are two ways to be far from the Father's heart.
You can rebel against Him by breaking every rule.
Or you can try to put Him in your debt by keeping them.
One says:
"I don't need the Father because I have pleasure."
The other says:
"I don't need grace because I have performance."
Both hearts need rescue.

This is why reducing Luke 15 to a sentimental story about a rebellious teenager misses part of Jesus' confrontation. The story responds to religious leaders who resented Jesus for welcoming sinners, and the father's response to both sons is central to the parable.
Jesus is confronting the person in the nightclub.
And the person in the pew.
The obvious sinner.
And the polished sinner.
The person ashamed of everything he has done.
And the person secretly proud of everything he hasn't done.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need Jesus.
Maybe you never had a dramatic far-country season.
Maybe your danger is subtler.
You read the story and think, "At least I never became like him."
Be careful.
That sentence sounds frighteningly similar to the older brother.
If another person's restoration irritates you...
If someone's testimony makes you compare rather than celebrate...
If you secretly believe certain sinners should have to crawl farther before Christians welcome their repentance...
If you love being known as righteous more than you love seeing sinners rescued...
Jesus may be exposing a far country located inside a religious heart.
And still the father goes out.
That is another breathtaking detail.
He runs toward the rebellious younger son.
He also goes out and appeals to the angry older son.
One was lost through rebellion.
One was endangered by self-righteousness.
The father moves toward both.
This is why Luke 15 refuses to let any of us stand safely outside the story.
Some of us wasted the inheritance.
Some of us resented the party.
Some of us have done both.
But the center of the story is not ultimately the impressive repentance of a son.
It is the astonishing mercy of the father.
That is why some commentators have noted that "the prodigal son" can be an inadequate title; the father's response occupies the theological center of the story.
And that changes how you hear it.
Because perhaps tonight you are sitting somewhere with a secret you have carried for years.
You think your worst chapter became your permanent name.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Backslider.
Liar.
Unclean.
Unworthy.
But Jesus Christ is not asking you to pretend that chapter never happened.
He is calling you to repent and surrender the pen.
That is the difference between cheap inspiration and the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely improve the ending of the old life.
He saves sinners and makes them new.
The scars may remain.
Consequences may remain.
Restitution may be necessary.
Relationships may require time to rebuild.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence of sin.
But your sin does not have greater saving power than Christ has redeeming power.
The cross is stronger than the accusation that says you can never return.
So stop rehearsing the speech that says you must earn your way into mercy.
You cannot purchase grace.
That is why it is grace.
Come to Christ honestly.
Come repentant.
Come empty-handed.
Come without pretending.
Come because Jesus still receives sinners.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs to hear that before they go to sleep tonight.
Someone smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Someone convinced God is finished with them.
Someone standing emotionally in a far country, wondering whether the road home is still open.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.
Not as a formula.
Not as public theater.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
But because sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops protecting the mask.
And if someone confesses struggle beneath this article, don't crush them.
Pray.
Encourage.
Point them toward Christ.
Remember the older brother.
The Church should never become a porch where restored prodigals are forced to explain why the Father let them inside.

Supporting Gospel Warrior is not a payment to God, and it does not buy spiritual favor. But financial support can be an act of Christian generosity and partnership when it helps biblical teaching reach more people.
And don't overlook the free resources.
But before you leave, go back to that road one more time.
See the boy.
No money.
No reputation.
No leverage.
No speech powerful enough to undo what he had done.
Just dust on his feet and repentance in his heart.
Now look farther down the road.
Someone is running.
That is the image Jesus wanted sinners—and religious people—to confront.
The son thought the defining fact about his life was what he had wasted.
The father believed the defining fact was that his son had come home.
And the Gospel takes us deeper still.
Our hope is not that we can somehow walk far enough back toward God to rescue ourselves.

Our hope is Jesus Christ—the One who came to seek and save the lost, who gave Himself for sinners, who rose victorious, and who calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and live as people transformed by grace.
So if you are still in the far country...
Come home.
If you are halfway down the road...
Keep coming.
If you are standing outside the celebration angry that grace reached somebody you thought deserved rejection...
Come inside.
There is no trophy for being the prodigal.
There is no trophy for being the older brother.
There is only grace for sinners who finally understand how desperately they need the Father.
Follow because we need truth more often than our algorithms naturally give it to us.
And remember this when shame whispers your old name:
You may remember yourself by the road you wasted your life on—but grace remembers there is still a road home.
